Rule-based observations from the findings below. Each one names the findings it rests on. There is no overall score and no verdict; provider assessments stay the provider\'s.

Registered only %1$s days ago. New domains are often used for phishing; this alone proves nothing.
No A or AAAA record: the name does not point to a server.
No CAA record: any certificate authority may issue certificates for it.
No DMARC policy: receiving servers get no instruction for spoofed mail.
No MX record: the domain does not receive e-mail.
No SPF record: anyone can send e-mail claiming to come from this domain.
No AlienVault OTX threat report mentions it.
Mentioned in %1$s AlienVault OTX threat report(s).
No answer from: %1$s. Run them again later.
Review: %1$s not reviewed, %2$s verified by you, %3$s marked conflicting.
Not on the Google Safe Browsing lists at query time.
SPF is soft (~all): mail from unlisted servers is only marked as suspicious.
SPF is strict (-all): mail from unlisted servers should be rejected.
SPF does not restrict senders (?all, +all or no all rule).
The domain is in a deletion phase (%1$s).

VirusTotal: no engine reports it as malicious or suspicious.

No version given: the list covers all versions, not necessarily yours.
OSINT-Book %1$s — GPL-3.0-or-later. Source code, licence and privacy notes are in the project repository.
Rate limited until %1$s; no request is sent before then.
At most three sources run at the same time. Findings that already arrived are kept if you stop.
Investigations are stored in the app\'s private storage and excluded from backups. The database itself is not additionally encrypted; API keys are encrypted with Android Keystore.
All investigations, notes, raw copies and saved API keys on this device will be deleted. Files you exported earlier are not affected and must be deleted separately.
Its targets, findings, notes, relations and local raw copies are removed. Reports or files you exported earlier are not deleted by this.
Delete %1$s together with its query runs and findings?
Community abuse reports for an IP address in the last 90 days, confidence score, provider (ISP) and usage type.
BigDataCloud: approximate location of an IP address with a confidence level (low, moderate, high), network owner and ASN. Shown on the map.
Public GitHub accounts, organisations and repositories: description, licence, languages, stars, dates and recent public repositories.
DNS records of a domain: IP addresses (A/AAAA), mail servers (MX), name servers (NS), TXT records such as SPF/DMARC, CNAME and CAA.
Approximate location of an IP address (country, region, city, coordinates), its network provider and ASN. Shown on the map.
abuse.ch MalwareBazaar: what is known about a file hash (malware family, file name and type, first and last seen, tags). No sample is downloaded or uploaded.
OpenStreetMap Nominatim: turns coordinates found for an IP into an approximate, city-level address. Runs only when you tap “Find approximate address”.
Known security vulnerabilities for a software package and version from the open OSV database.
AlienVault Open Threat Exchange: threat intelligence pulses that mention a domain or IP, plus ASN and country.
Checks whether a host answers ping and measures round-trip time and packet loss with four echo requests.
Registration data from the official registry: registrar, creation and expiry dates, status, name servers; for IP addresses the network range, owner organisation and country.
Google Safe Browsing: whether a link or domain is currently on Google\'s malware, phishing or unwanted-software lists.
abuse.ch URLhaus: whether a domain, IP or URL is listed as distributing malware, with threat type, status and tags. Lookup only.
urlscan.io: earlier public scans of a domain or IP, with page URL, server, IP and country. The app only searches; it never submits new scans.
Existing VirusTotal reports for a domain, URL or IP: how many security engines flagged it, categories and network owner. Nothing is uploaded for scanning.
First, last and closest archived snapshot of a site in the Internet Archive\'s Wayback Machine.
Matching Wikipedia articles and Wikidata entities for an organisation or name, for context.

Saved or shared files leave the app\'s protected storage and may leave this device. Deleting the investigation later does not delete them. API keys are never included.
Sends these coordinates to nominatim.openstreetmap.org and saves the city-level address it returns as a new finding.
IP location is an estimate of where the network is registered or routed (often the provider\'s city). It is not the location of a person or device; sources may disagree.

Off by default. When on, provider responses are stored locally for 30 days so their SHA-256 can be re-checked. Only use this where the provider\'s terms allow caching.

This provider only answers with a personal API key. Create a free account with the provider and enter your key in Settings; everything else works without it.
Your key is saved and encrypted with Android Keystore. To replace it, delete it and enter the new one.
Paste the key here. It stays encrypted on this device.
No coordinates yet. Query an IP address with ipwho.is or ipapi.co to place it on the map.

No connection. Saved investigations, notes and reports still work; queries need a network.
Collect public information about domains, URLs, IP addresses, organisations, repositories and packages, keep it with its sources and turn it into a report.
No account, no cloud, no tracking or ads. Investigations stay in the app\'s private storage and are excluded from backups.
Nothing is sent until you start a query. The search value and your device\'s IP address then reach that provider, under its own terms. You see what goes where before each query.
Queries go straight to the sources you choose
No port scanning, exploitation, login bypass or person profiling. A provider\'s risk label is its view, not a verdict.
Pinch with two fingers or double-tap a page to zoom.

Stored locally: investigations, targets, findings, notes, relations; optionally raw responses (30 days). Encrypted with Android Keystore: your API keys. Sent to a provider only when you start a query: the target value it needs and your IP address. Never collected: contacts, location, files, clipboard, browsing history, analytics. Export creates files only where you save or share them. Public availability of information does not make unlimited republishing of personal data acceptable.
Maps: when a map is on screen, map tiles for that area are loaded from tile.openstreetmap.org.

This report lists information as returned by the named sources at the stated times. Same names or addresses do not by themselves mean the same person or owner. SHA-256 values detect later changes to local copies; they do not prove that the information is correct.
Passive queries to the public sources listed below, started by the user. Each finding keeps its source link and retrieval time. Latest run per source and target:
Sources without results in their latest run: %1$s
No overall risk score is computed; each source\'s assessment is shown separately.
Risk labels from this source are its own assessment, not a verdict of this app.
Ready to use. Turn a source off if you do not want queries to go to it.

These sources answer only with your own free API key. A key is like a personal password for the service: you create it on the provider\'s website, paste it here once, and it is stored encrypted on this device only. It is never put into reports or exports. Everything else in the app works without keys.

Detects changes to a local copy. It does not prove the content is true.

1. Open auth.abuse.ch and sign in with one of the offered accounts (for example GitHub or Google). It is free.
2. In your profile, find “Optional: API Keys” and generate an Auth-Key.
3. Copy the key and paste it below.
The same abuse.ch key works for both URLhaus and MalwareBazaar; paste it into each.

1. Create a free account at abuseipdb.com/register and confirm your e-mail.
2. Sign in and open Account → API (abuseipdb.com/account/api).
3. Tap “Create Key” and give it a name such as “OSINT phone”.
4. Copy the key and paste it below.
The free plan allows 1,000 IP checks per day.

1. Create a free account at bigdatacloud.com (Sign up) and confirm your e-mail.
2. Sign in and open your Account page; your API key is listed under “API Keys”.
3. Copy the key and paste it below.
The free plan has a monthly quota; the provider's page shows how much is left.

1. Sign in at github.com (a free account is enough).
2. Open Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens.
3. Tap “Generate new token”, give it a name and choose “Public repositories (read-only)”. No other permissions are needed.
4. Generate, copy the token (starts with github_pat_) and paste it below.
Without a key GitHub allows 60 requests per hour; with one, 5,000.

1. Sign up for free at otx.alienvault.com and confirm your e-mail.
2. Sign in and open your profile (top right) → Settings.
3. Copy the value shown under “OTX Key”.
4. Paste it below.

1. Open console.cloud.google.com and sign in with a Google account. No payment method is needed for this API.
2. Create a project (or pick one).
3. Go to APIs & Services → Library, search for “Safe Browsing API” and tap Enable.
4. Go to APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → API key.
5. Optionally restrict the key to the Safe Browsing API, then copy it and paste it below.
Google allows the Lookup API for non-commercial use.

Search works without a key at a low limit. For a higher limit:
1. Create a free account at urlscan.io/user/signup.
2. Open Settings & API → “New API key”.
3. Copy the key and paste it below.

1. Open virustotal.com and choose “Sign up” to create a free community account.
2. Confirm your e-mail address and sign in.
3. Open your profile menu (top right) → “API key”.
4. Copy the key and paste it below.
The free public API allows 4 requests per minute and 500 per day, for non-commercial use.
No version given: results may concern any version of the package.
Private or reserved address: public sources usually know nothing about it.
